definition: The 'People of the Goddess Danu', a race of skilled and divine beings in Irish tradition who are said to have ruled Ireland before the Milesians. Medieval writers often treated them as ancient kings or as the people of the sídhe mounds.
An Irish word meaning 'cattle raid', and the name of a whole genre of tales built around the theft of cattle. The most famous is Táin Bó Cúailnge, the Cattle Raid of Cooley.

A group of medieval Irish tales about the Ulaid, the people of Ulster, and their heroes Conchobar and Cú Chulainn. The cycle survives in manuscripts such as the Book of the Dun Cow and the Book of Leinster.

The body of tales about Fionn mac Cumhaill, his warrior band the Fianna, and the poet Oisín. Much of it is framed as Oisín's recollections to St Patrick in Acallam na Senórach, and it continued in later ballads and folklore.

A parallel realm of gods, spirits and the dead in Celtic storytelling, often reached through mounds, lakes or across the sea. It is usually a place of youth, music and abundance, but it runs on its own sense of time.
A binding taboo or obligation laid on a hero, often at birth or by a powerful figure. Breaking a geas is thought to bring disaster, and many Irish tales turn on a hero trapped between two of them.

A learned specialist in ritual, law, memory and prophecy in Celtic societies, described by classical authors and appearing in Irish tales as an adviser to kings. Druids such as Cathbad read omens and pronounce on the future.
A professional poet-seer in Irish tradition, trained for years in genealogy, law, praise poetry and storytelling. The fili held high status, and a satire from a poet was feared as a kind of curse.

A war-goddess of Irish tradition, whose name is often translated 'phantom queen'. She is associated with fate, battle and sovereignty, appears as a crow, and is sometimes described as one of a trio of sisters.

The 'Land of the Young', an Otherworld island of eternal youth, beauty and plenty in Irish tradition. It is ruled or associated with Manannán mac Lir, and Niamh brings Oisín there in the Fenian tales.
